quotes.t: The lack of money is the root of all evil.
October. This is one of the peculiarly dangerous months to speculate in stocks. The others are July, January, September, April, November, May, March, June, December, August, and February.
All you need in this life is ignorance and confidence, and then success is sure.
Beliefs have the power to create and the power to destroy.
Nothing in life has any meaning except the meaning you give it.
It is not about your resources, it is about your resourcefulness.
The meaning of my existence is that life has addressed a question to me.
Life has always seemed to me like a plant that lives on its rhizome. Its true life is invisible, hidden in the rhizome.

The dream is the small hidden door in the deepest and most intimate sanctum of the soul, which opens to that primeval cosmic night that was soul long before there was conscious ego and will be soul far beyond what a conscious ego could ever reach.
Out of the huts of history's shame, I rise.
quotes.source: Still I Rise, from And Still I Rise (1978)

quotes.t: You may trod me in the very dirt, but still, like dust, I'll rise.
quotes.source: Still I Rise, from And Still I Rise (1978)

quotes.t: Develop enough courage so that you can stand up for yourself and then stand up for somebody else.
The artist is the creator of beautiful things. To reveal art and conceal the artist is art's aim.
quotes.source: The Picture of Dorian Gray, Preface (1891)

quotes.t: Those who find beautiful meanings in beautiful things are the cultivated. For these there is hope.
quotes.source: The Picture of Dorian Gray, Preface (1891)

quotes.t: All art is quite useless.
quotes.source: The Picture of Dorian Gray, Preface (1891)

quotes.t: Victory attained by violence is tantamount to a defeat, for it is momentary.
Nonviolence is the first article of my faith. It is also the last article of my creed.
An unjust law is itself a species of violence. Arrest for its breach is more so.
Let us therefore brace ourselves to our duties, and so bear ourselves that, if the British Empire and its Commonwealth last for a thousand years, men will still say, This was their finest hour.
From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.
Victory at all costs, victory in spite of all terror, victory, however long and hard the road may be; for without victory, there is no survival.
Do not pursue the taste of good food.
Do not collect weapons or practice with weapons beyond what is useful.
Do not seek to possess either goods or fiefs for your old age.
What I am looking for is not out there, it is in me.
Joy is the holy fire that keeps our purpose warm and our intelligence aglow.
Many persons have a wrong idea of what constitutes true happiness. It is not attained through self-gratification but through fidelity to a worthy purpose.
Attack him where he is unprepared, appear where you are not expected.
The general who wins a battle makes many calculations in his temple before the battle is fought. The general who loses a battle makes but few calculations beforehand.
Water shapes its course according to the nature of the ground over which it flows; the soldier works out his victory in relation to the foe whom he is facing.
If anybody dreams of the exclusive survival of his own religion and the destruction of the others, I pity him from the bottom of my heart.
quotes.source: Address at the Final Session, Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 27 September 1893

quotes.t: Holiness, purity and charity are not the exclusive possessions of any church in the world, and every system has produced men and women of the most exalted character.
quotes.source: Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 1893

quotes.t: It fills my heart with joy unspeakable to rise in response to the warm and cordial welcome which you have given us.
quotes.source: Response to Welcome, Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 11 September 1893

quotes.t: Painting is poetry that is seen rather than felt, and poetry is painting that is felt rather than seen.
Nature is the source of all true knowledge.
He who does not value life does not deserve it.
The ignited mind of the youth is the most powerful resource on the earth, above the earth and under the earth.
Have courage to think differently, courage to invent, to travel the unexplored path, courage to discover the impossible and to conquer the problems and succeed.
Success is when your signature changes to autograph.
What I know for sure is that what you give comes back to you.
When you undervalue what you do, the world will undervalue who you are.
Be thankful for what you have; you'll end up having more. If you concentrate on what you don't have, you will never, ever have enough.
Courage is more exhilarating than fear and in the long run it is easier.
The giving of love is an education in itself.
Since you get more joy out of giving joy to others, you should put a good deal of thought into the happiness that you are able to give.
Man is not the creature of circumstances; circumstances are the creatures of men.
There is no education like adversity.
The most successful man in life is the man who has the best information.
Art is the elimination of the unnecessary.
There is no abstract art. You must always start with something. Afterward you can remove all traces of reality.
The world today doesn't make sense, so why should I paint pictures that do?

Education is the great engine of personal development. It is through education that the daughter of a peasant can become a doctor, that the son of a mineworker can become the head of the mine, that a child of farm workers can become the president of a great nation.
No country can really develop unless its citizens are educated.
Courageous people do not fear forgiving, for the sake of peace.
What is great in man is that he is a bridge and not an end.
No one can construct for you the bridge upon which precisely you must cross the stream of life, no one but you yourself alone.
We have art in order not to die of the truth.
The supreme function of reason is to show man that some things are beyond reason.
Thought constitutes the greatness of man.
It is not from space that I must seek my dignity, but from the government of my thought.
A man is not idle because he is absorbed in thought. There is visible labor and there is invisible labor.
Prayer is not asking. Prayer is putting oneself in the hands of God, at His disposition, and listening to His voice in the depth of our hearts.
There are more things to admire in men than to despise.
Life is very short, and there's no time for fussing and fighting, my friend.
I was not born to join in hatred, but in love.
The worst sin towards our fellow creatures is not to hate them, but to be indifferent to them: that's the essence of inhumanity.
An army marches on its stomach.
Until he extends his circle of compassion to all living things, man will not himself find peace.
Compassion for others begins with kindness to ourselves.
Worthless people live only to eat and drink; people of worth eat and drink only to live.
Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth.
Enlightenment is like the moon reflected on the water. The moon does not get wet, nor is the water broken.
Work keeps at bay three great evils: boredom, vice, and need.
Necessity is the mother of invention.
A moment comes, which comes but rarely in history, when we step out from the old to the new, when an age ends, and when the soul of a nation, long suppressed, finds utterance.
We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny.
Wild nights! Wild nights! Were I with thee, wild nights should be our luxury!
I have been bent and broken, but — I hope — into a better shape.
He that can have patience can have what he will.
I've always loved you, and when you love someone, you love the whole person, just as he or she is, and not as you would like them to be.
There could have been no two hearts so open, no tastes so similar, no feelings so in unison, no countenances so beloved.
Above all, don't lie to yourself.
Goodness is stronger than evil. Love is stronger than hate. Light is stronger than darkness.
Whoever is happy will make others happy too.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: The only abnormality is the incapacity to love.
I am rooted, but I flow.
Do the Duty which lies nearest thee, which thou knowest to be a Duty! Thy second Duty will already have become clearer.
You can't connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backwards.
Fortune is like glass—the brighter the glitter, the more easily broken.
No one can conceive the variety of feelings which bore me onwards, like a hurricane, in the first enthusiasm of success.
Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.
I have no more made my book than my book has made me.
Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world.
When a man is tired of London, he is tired of life; for there is in London all that life can afford.
Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
Much have I travelled in the realms of gold.
quotes.source: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer

quotes.t: I care for myself. The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself.
I am Heathcliff!
Fear of danger is ten thousand times more terrifying than danger itself.
The secret of a great success for which you are at a loss to account is a crime that has never been found out, because it was properly executed.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Alexander Pope.bio: English poet and master of the heroic couplet. His works include An Essay on Criticism, The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man, along with celebrated translations of Homer.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Carl Jung.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. His concepts of the collective unconscious, archetypes and introversion and extraversion remain influential in psychology and culture.
Carl Jung.credit: AnonymousUnknown author, Public domain (File: File:CARL JUNG (1875 - 1961).jpg)

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Daniel Defoe.bio: English writer, journalist and spy (1660-1731), best known for the novel Robinson Crusoe (1719).

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Emily Brontë.bio: Emily Brontë was an English novelist and poet whose single novel, Wuthering Heights, is a strange and powerful story of love and revenge on the Yorkshire moors. Intensely private, she published under the name Ellis Bell and died at thirty.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Honoré de Balzac.bio: French novelist and playwright (1799-1850), author of the sequence of novels and stories La Comédie humaine.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Mark Twain.bio: American writer (Samuel Clemens) known for Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Michel de Montaigne.bio: French Renaissance writer who popularized the essay as a literary form.
Michel de Montaigne.credit: Engraving by J. C. G. Fritzsch, Public domain

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Percy Bysshe Shelley.bio: Percy Bysshe Shelley was an English Romantic poet, author of Ozymandias, Adonais and Prometheus Unbound, and a leading voice of Romanticism.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Samuel Johnson.bio: Samuel Johnson was an English writer who compiled the first great Dictionary of the English Language in 1755. Poet, essayist and the most quoted conversationalist of his age, his life was immortalised in Boswell's famous biography.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Søren Kierkegaard.bio: Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher and theologian regarded as the first existentialist thinker. Writing under playful pseudonyms, he explored faith, anxiety and the individual's leap beyond rational systems in works such as Fear and Trembling.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Tony Robbins.bio: Tony Robbins is an American author, coach and motivational speaker known for bestselling books such as Unlimited Power and Awaken the Giant Within. His seminars and self-help programmes have made him one of the most prominent figures in the personal development industry.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
